ownedComment.body:
The key to understanding the Strategy view is to realize that a strategy is not everything. It sits in an environment of information and ideas, often in the heads of stakeholders. A strategy is simply one element, although an essential one.
The business model describes how the business is supposed to be, but often it does not describe how it currently is. This can happen because the model was changed by executives, but the company is taking time to adapt and change to the new model. Or, perhaps, the model is an idealistic view, while the actual organization is exactly optimum.
A strategy, then, can define changes to the organization either for the purpose of making it more like the business model (to complete a transition) or less like the operating model (to optimize for reality). Regardless of why a strategy exists, is always exists in the context of the business model.

properties.documentation: The concerns package is an effort to map out the various stakeholders for the model and the concerns that each of the stakeholder communities would have. As this is a reference model, the stakeholders are not specific people, but rather "typical" roles in business and IT settings.

element.name: Stakeholders and Concerns for Enterprise Business Motivation Model

properties.documentation: The mind map of stakeholders and concerns is an attempt to capture the array of stakeholders for the EBMM and the concerns that we would like to address through the development of the EBMM.

element.name: Stakeholder: Business Unit Mgrs Ops, Finance, Mfg, Logistics)

properties.documentation: Business executives are unlikely to deal directly with the information stored in an instantiation of the EBMM. Rather, advisors and analysts would use the model to manage information that could be used to produce recommendations (or raw observations) for the consumption of the business executive. Their concerns, as entered here, are therefore indirect. These are the concerns of the business executive that an advisor or analyst would need to be able to meet.

element.name: Able to track progress against plans

properties.documentation: In order to create a basis for governance and value realization, IT resources need to be able to track progress of delivery and readiness towards corporate goals.

IT Stakeholders need to be able to answer key questions posed by their senior staff, even when it is not clear why those questions are being asked. These include:
  • What technologies should we be investing in, and why?
  • Is our staff trained and ready to use and support the necessary technologies?
  • How many applications are in our portfolio and how many will be there in a year?
  • What strategic outcomes are most impacted by actual events of: downtime, information integrity problems, and delivery delays.
  • How much of the IT budget is being invested in creating new enterprise abilities vs. keeping the lights on?
  • How many systems are candidates for consolidation? When will their future be determined?
Business unit managers need to be confident that the choices that they make are not likely to delay a needed change beyond its expected window of opportunity.

element.name: Basis for Governance and Value Realization

properties.documentation: IT stakeholders need to be able to demonstrate that activities funded to take place in the IT unit are producing the expected business value. As projects proceed, the relative connection to business value and/or business strategy is used to create prioritization, govern activities, and measure resulting value.

While business executives typically do not need business assessments to be modeled, the modeling of business assessments is useful to the rest of the enterprise when fulfilling the strategies produced to respond to those business assessments.

element.name: Connect Business Rules to Business Motivation

properties.documentation: Business Rules create overhead. Tying rules to business motivation allows the value of the rules to be clearly balanced against the cost.

element.name: Connect Metrics and Measures to Business Strategies

properties.documentation: Business Process Stakeholders need to have a clear map of the value chain, indicating the mechanisms by which information, resources, materials, parts, and products flow in order to establish a uniform measurement regimen.

element.name: Create "imperative" focus areas to realize strategy

properties.documentation: Often called "heat-mapping," this activity involves mining the enterprise architecture information to find the capabilities that are necessary for the realization of a strategy, and then to call attention to the subset of capabilities where their maturity or performance must be improved.

Business Rules Practitioners need to have a complete map of business processes where a specific business rule needs to be implemented. This allows the rules expert to insure that the rules are understood and implemented in a consistent manner.

The sometimes competing, and often confusing, mechanisms by which strategies are grouped, analyzed, communicated, funded, and effected can produce unintended delays, poor resource allocation, and failure to recognize the strategic importance of specific activities. When used correctly, the model can provide a consistent nomenclature for describing the various business models at play in an enterprise, and for communicating the strategies related to each of those business models. This will not prevent contention, but it should reduce confusion and delay.

In order to provide reasonable services for business, IT Stakeholders need to be able to create roadmaps to support feasible initiatives. The EBMM should provide all the necessary elements to model these roadmaps so that "roadmap collision" can be avoided.

Every team must make priorities and follow through in order to deliver their change efforts within budget. However, those priorities need to be aligned so that the work being done is actually the work that needs to be done. Information useful for creating a clear list of priorities is extraordinarily helpful to business leaders.
Business unit managers would like to be made aware of opportunities that may exist to leverage the investments and success of other teams.

element.name: Focus effort on improving the most strategic business processes

properties.documentation: Business Process Practitioners need to know which business processes are most closely aligned to strategic requirements in order to focus limited business process improvement resources on the most valuable processes.

In order to insure that business services are well understood, well delivered, and well utilized, IT professionals need to understand the incentives that motivate the business and, if possible, should be able to recommend updates to those incentives that would foster positive benefits.

IT Stakeholders need to understand the relationships between business and business motivations in order to insure that business requirements do not have gaps that could affect the timely delivery of appropriate and feasible value.

Business Rules Practitioners need to insure that standards are followed in the creation and description of business rules. Capturing the business rules of the organization in a consistent manner is a necessary component to governing their creation and execution.
The EBMM should provide for a location for storing the list of architectural risks and issues, along with status information (captures, events, exceptions, escalations, documentation links, etc).

Business unit managers need to not only make changes, but to do so in full view of the risks and potential consequences of their choices. If a decision is risky, they need to know it before the decision is made and they need to feel comfortable that trusted individuals are working to mitigate the risks.

Business unit managers need to feel comfortable that the path that they have chosen to take is not likely to incur undue costs of change. In other words, if it will be expensive to make a change, every effort should be made to narrow the costs, spread them out, reduce risks, and prepare careful budgets so that there are no surprises.

element.name: Prioritize Service Mgmt Improvements using Bus. Drivers

properties.documentation: The ability to connect service management to business motivation is most often used to recognize the relative prioritization of specific change requests on the basis of the relative importance of an IT service. This requires weighted mapping from business services to the business units that consume them.
IT Stakeholders need to be able to represent their offerings as business services in order to support the ability to describe the accumulation of value from a service.

element.name: Represent an accurate view of business motivation

properties.documentation: In order to provide a basis for governance and value realization, IT stakeholders need to be able to demonstrate clear lines from strategic needs to actual project investments.
Advisors to senior leaders need accurate and consumable analysis about the company, its competitors, and opportunities for excellence in order to suggest appropriate strategies to go after.

element.name: Trace Business Services to Business Models

properties.documentation: IT Stakeholders need to be able to trace the business services that they offer to the business models of the company. This allows many things, including the correct allocation of benefits to profit centers (for proper service funding) and the correct calculation of business impact of service outage (for proper prioritization during problem mgmt).

From the EA standpoint, the model should provide a simple and understandable mechanism for demonstrating that specific business activities are (or are not) inspired by business strategies and goals. Typically, this involves the modeling of business strategies and creating mappings to the capabilities of the business that are impacted by them.

element.name: Traceability from strategies to change requests

properties.documentation: IT Stakeholders need to prioritize the change requests against limits in resource availability. Traceability to strategy is useful because it allows IT stakeholders to clearly describe the relative importance of specific change requests to business stakeholders, allowing one business customer to accept the need to defer their goals in order to support the needs of another business customer.

element.name: Understandable to Business Stakeholders of EA

properties.documentation: The EBMM must describe concepts and relationships in a manner that aligns with common usage within business organizations. In order to capture the notion of "common usage," the authors are relying on the use of terminology as described in mass-marketed business materials as well as terms introduced in college level business courses.
Enterprise Architecture needs a model that is useful for supporting the management of information.
Enterprise Architecture stakeholders need a model that is useful for enterprise portfolio and demand management.
Value Chain Viewpoint
Enterprise Business Motivation Model v 5.0, August 2014, A. Nicklas Malik
Business Driver Viewpoint
Service Management Viewpoint
IT Traceability Viewpoint
Business Model Assessment Viewpoint
Primary Viewpoint
Customer view is coauthored by Mike Clark

The business model describes how the business is supposed to be, but often it does not describe how it currently is. This can happen because the model was changed by executives, but the company is taking time to adapt and change to the new model. Or, perhaps, the model is an idealistic view, while the actual organization is exactly optimum.
A strategy, then, can define changes to the organization either for the purpose of making it more like the business model (to complete a transition) or less like the operating model (to optimize for reality). A type of business construct, a technical construct is a composition of elements usually used in technology-focused settings.

A structured collection of concepts and relationships useful for sharing a common understanding about a business. A construct is made of specific business elements related in a specific way. A model is a type of construct that is useful for creating a complete understanding of a particular subject from a particular viewpoint.
A part of a business construct or model that describes one aspect of a business, usually from a particular viewpoint.

A business tool composed of one or more software components that, together, serve a business purpose. Applications are able to create or use the data objects that make up a business transaction. They may use one or more software platforms. To be used, they must be deployed on a host.

Independently tracked risk or issue observable in the architecture. Typically captured by an Enterprise Architect. This entity may contain links to documentation of the risk, escalations, exceptions, status, events, and quantifiable measures.

When a capability is defined in an organization, there are expectations of the level of performance or maturity required in order for the business to be successful in their mission. An assessment metric defines a way in which a set of capabilities will be measured. For example, if all capabilities will be measured on the basis of their value, performance, and maturity (VPM), then there are three assessment metrics. Capturing the measures for an assessment metric is a key element of business architecture. The measurement process must be consistent and, in the best case, should reference widely accepted business measurement practices. In order for cross-enterprise assessment to take place in a timely and effective manner, it is a best practice for a single team to define a standard set of capability assessment metrics that will be used by every individual that performs the analysis. Assessment measures are used to help the business to
  1. visualize the gaps between expected and actual performance,
  2. place appropriate prioritization on the capabilities that need attention, and
  3. evaluate the current allocation of resources in budgets and program alignments to the areas with the greatest gaps.
In other words, if ten capabilities are important to enabling a strategy, the data related to their required performance and maturity can assist the organization in deciding which one of those capabilities should receive investment in order to be effective fulfilling the strategy. Some examples of assessment metrics may include: the business-perceived value of a capability, the level of expected performance against a particular set of key performance indicators (KPIs), the incidence rate of defects or variations, the incremental and overall cost of providing the capability, the number of resources involved, the level of automation and/or integration, the risk of business interruption (for disaster recovery) and the likelihood of customer impact if performance metrics change.

An asset is a generalization of property owned by the enterprise. It is included in the extended views of this model because the concept of asset is included in the models from which this model is derived. Assets are described in the extended views of the OMG BMM as well as the TOGAF metamodel. In the context of this model, an asset is any property controlled by a business unit through a business process. The management of that asset is subject to the constraints created by business directives.
In the EBMM, Assets do not include people since people are not property. Tools are shown as a subtype of asset, and applications are a subtype of tools. Be aware that not all organizations manage their IT applications as corporate assets.

Porter's Five Forces analysis looks at individual businesses or "strategic business units", examining the threats that lead to a rich understanding of the competitive and cooperative environment in which a business operates.
  • Economies of scale e.g. the benefits associated with bulk purchasing.
  • The high or low cost of entry e.g. how much will it cost for the latest technology?
  • Ease of access to distribution channels e.g. Do our competitors have the distribution channels sewn up?
  • Cost advantages not related to the size of the company e.g. personal contacts or knowledge that larger companies do not own or learning curve effects.
  • Will competitors retaliate?
  • Government action e.g. will new laws be introduced that will weaken our competitive position?
  • How important is differentiation? e.g. The Champagne brand cannot be copied. This desensitises the influence of the environment.
  • This is high where there a few, large players in a market e.g. the large grocery chains.
  • If there are a large number of undifferentiated, small suppliers e.g. small farming businesses supplying the large grocery chains.
  • The cost of switching between suppliers is low e.g. from one fleet supplier of trucks to another.
A series of customer impressions and expectations about the value of an offering based on the branding associated with that offering.

A carefully constructed series of commitments made by the maker of a product or service that lives under a brand. A brand promise helps the customer form an accurate brand impression. Examples would include: "top quality," "rarely breaks," "adapts to fit my lifestyle," "lowest cost," "works in unusual ways," "represents advanced thinking," "aligns with my values and/or political opinions," etc.

In the EBMM, a business capability is an abstraction that represents the ability of a business unit to perform a particular business function or process. Used primarily for analysis and model navigation, this abstraction is normally considered to be a composition of processes, people, tools, and information.
A single business unit normally has many business capabilities. Evaluations of maturity take place against a business capability within the context of each business unit that implements it, because only a business unit can provide the resources and processes that are needed to perform a business capability.
Until a business capability is mapped to a business unit, it is purely conceptual. It may be desirable. But it cannot be performed. Mapping a business capability to a business unit answers the question "who is accountable to execute it?" but not the question "how will it be executed?" That requires one more mapping, this time from the capability to the business process.

A business capability taxonomy is an ordered hierarchy of business capabilities, structured in a manner that makes sense to the stakeholders, and used to create associations between capabilities and business units.
Note that a relationship to a capability is seen as a relationship to one, many, or all of the capabilities contained within it in the hierarchy. This ability to make "loose" associations is useful to reduce the difficulty of mapping activities.
A business capability is a conceptual "element" of a business. In many ways, a capability is the basic building block of a business in the same way that atoms and molecules are the building blocks of matter.
A business capability is a stable component of the business architecture describing "what" a company does, whereupon a business process describes "how" it does it, and a business model describes "why" it does it. It is important, when creating a business architectural model, to keep these three interrogatives independent of one another.
A business capability is implemented by process, people, technology and information. Business capabilities provide a stable anchor point as process re-engineering, sourcing and technology optimization occur. Linking business capabilities to strategies drives prioritization and focus enabling efficient and effective execution.
Note: when discussing the notion of business capabilities to enterprise architects who are familiar with the Zachman Framework, you will <u>not </u>find consensus on where this conceptual element belongs. This bothers some folks because the Zachman Framework is often compared to the Periodic Table of Elements in chemistry. Every element must be found in the Periodic table. Hence, the argument goes, capabilities do not exist because they are not in the table.
The authors of the EBMM believe that this argument is simple to address, using the same metaphor.
Where the Zachman framework describes the "atoms" of a business, the capabilities are a type of molecule. And just as the Periodic table of elements does not illustrate a chart of molecules, the Zachman Framework does not illustrate a chart of capabilities.
So the next time someone asks "why aren't capabilities in the Zachman Framework," simply reply with a similar question: "why isn't caffeine in the Periodic Table of Elements?"

A Goal is a statement about a state or condition of the enterprise to be brought about or sustained through appropriate Means. A Goal amplifies a Vision - that is, it indicates what must be satisfied on a continuing basis to effectively attain the Vision. A Goal should be narrow - focused enough that it can be quantified by success metrics. A Vision, in contrast, is too broad or grand for it to be specifically measured directly by success metrics. However, determining whether a statement is a Vision or a Goal is often impossible without in-depth knowledge of the context and intent of the business planners. Compared to an success metric, a Goal tends to be longer term, qualitative (rather than quantitative), general (rather than specific), and ongoing. Compared to a Goal, an success metric tends to be short term, quantitative (rather than qualitative), specific (rather than general), and not continuing beyond its time frame (which may be cyclical). (Derived from OMG Business Motivation Model 1.0)

A model illustrating the groupings and relationships between the data elements that make up business documents. Since a business document is a special case of a data object that represents a business transaction, the business information model is a proxy, at the information level, for modeling the relationships between the business transactions themselves.

A chartered (or proposed) project or ongoing group of projects designed to change the structure, capabilities, or performance of the enterprise. Typically, initiatives are chartered to create a measurable improvement in a business capability, often through process improvement, technology improvement, structural change (reorganization, insourcing / outsourcing, etc), or accountability changes (governance, reporting, scorecarding, incentives).

A generalization of the elements of a business model assessment. The types of business judgments include strengths, weaknesses, issues, recommended changes, and potential impacts (risks and rewards). The business model assessment is composed of one or more business judgments, and puts perspective around the model or models evaluated. This section of the model specifically supports the use of SWOT analysis to provide insight into a business model.

A business model is a composition of business elements that represents the value proposition, products, customer demands, competencies, partnerships and distribution channels that a business will employ in order to deliver value.

A business model assessment is an artifact or document that contains an analysis of one (or more) of the business models of an enterprise. It may be formal, with hundreds or thousands of typed pages, or informal, delivered to an executive over lunch at the golf course. Business model assessments are composed of a set of judgments about one or more influencers that affect the organizations ability to execute on the existing business model. Business judgements are produced as the result of an assessment process, which is an examination of one or more of the business models in use in the enterprise in light of a dynamic business environment. Business judgements in the business model assessment may motivate the creation of principles, goals and/or strategies that either directly modify the business model or influence how the model is being executed upon.
Any device, tool, system, machine, or other reusable asset that is needed by an actor in the performance of a business process. A computer application is one type of tool.
A partner to the enterprise, usually another enteprise that benefits from a relationship with the enterprise in question.

Formally documented management expectations and intentions. Policies are used to direct decisions, and to ensure consistent and appropriate development and implementation of Processes, Standards, Roles, Activities, IT Infrastructure etc.

documentation.value: Type of the Business policy: performance, compliance, behavior, control, standard, etc

properties.documentation:
A business process is a collection of activities that take one or more inputs and transform them into process outputs in support of a desired business outcome that is of value to customers and/or partners. A business outcome may include a product, service, transaction, agreement, report, plan or strategy etc, and may benefit customers, suppliers, regulators, owners, clients or partners. Implications and Discussion of the term business process:
  • The activities are collected in a series. This implies flow, from one activity to another, and whenever possible, processes will be described with an indication of the sequence in which the activities are to occur.
  • A process is defined in terms of the process output. Usually the first step in describing a business process, or even recognizing when a business process exists, is to identify the output or deliverable from that process. Lacking an output, it is not possible to define or improve a business process in a useful or measurable manner.
The definition of the term 'activity' is important because a business process may be decomposed into a collection of activities. In this model, both are modeled with the same element due to this decompositional nature. The Workflow Management Coalition (WfMC) defines 'activity' as follows:
  • An activity is a description of a piece of work that forms one logical step within a process. An activity may be a manual activity, which does not support computer automation, or a workflow (automated) activity. A workflow activity requires human and/or machine resources(s) to support process execution; where human resource is required an activity is allocated to a workflow participant.
This model will use the term Activity as defined by the WfMC, to indicate a single logical step in a process. The flow of a process can include other processes, sub-processes and activities. An activity is not, in and of itself, a sub-process. Using the label "activity" indicates that the modeler believes that the item in question is a single logical step.

A business process taxonomy is an ordered hierarchy of business processes where each level down the hierarchy is thought to include a more detailed description of each element in the upper hierarchy. The top levels of the taxonomy are often unordered groups where no actual sequence exists between the sub-elements anywhere in the enterprise.
A condition or capability that must be met or possessed by an application to satisfy the stated or implicit needs of a business process.
A set of responsibilities that can be assigned to, and performed by, a person. A person may have more than one role, and may have a role for a short period of time.

Business rules and Facts describe the operations, definitions and constraints that apply to an organization in achieving its goal. A rule is an expression, in structured natural language, that uses business terms to describe a policy in a clear and testable manner. As an expression of business policy, rules clearly define the constraints to both human and system behavior necessary for the business to behave in an intentional and well governed manner.

A management tool, usually presented as a report, that illustrates a set of carefully chosen metrics designed to provide useful feedback on the health and alignment of the enterprise. One type of business scorecard is a "Balanced Scorecard," referring to a concept developed by Drs. Robert Kaplan (Harvard Business School) and David Norton. A Balanced Scorecard enables a Strategy to be broken down into Key Performance Indicators. Performance against the KPIs is used to demonstrate how well the Strategy is being achieved. A Balanced Scorecard has 4 major areas, each of which has a small number of KPIs. The same 4 areas are considered at different levels of detail throughout the Organisation.

A collection of business capabilities, offered as the external offerings of a single business unit, and made available to one or more customers. The customers may be internal (within the enterprise) or external. The ITIL definition of 'business service' is a synonym for Business Service, and is defined as: a Service that is delivered to Business Customers by Business Units. For example, delivery of financial services to Customers of a bank, or goods to the Customers of a retail store. Successful delivery of Business Services often depends on one or more IT Services. (ITIL v3) Note that the 'products' offered by the business service are not the same as the 'capabilities' of that service.

Strategy is a complex set of related statements used to motivate the creation of projects, the setting of goals, and the achievement of objectives by employees and partners of an enterprise in support of a business goal. It is not a course of action in itself, but a instead provides the general outlines of a course of action sufficient to drive specific changes in business operations. Strategies are defined in terms of objectives.
A strategy motivates change. It is the means by which an goal is to be reached. Rarely a statement of continuity, a strategy describes one or more specific changes that should be made to the enterprise. Those changes may be made to any element of the enterprise, including to the business model, the business capabilities, the structure of the business units, and even the technologies used to manage information.
A strategy may enable another strategy (If the widget department meets their objectives, then we can drop our reworking costs by 15% in the third month.)
In addition, a strategy may influence another strategy: ("With the push for quality in the widget division, the thingamabob division has set new goals for 2012.").
Strategies may be inspired directly by influencers like competitive pressure or business trends or they may be suggested in a business model assessment. It is important to know the source of the strategy and what it is responding to, in order to understand relative importance and check the assumptions on which a strategy is based.
A strategy may operate at any level of the organization from the most broadly encompassing enterprise wide level to the department or team level.

A business term is an term used within an enterprise as part of the vocabulary of terms for the business. Business rule expressions make use of business terms to communicate specific and measurable expectations of behavior. For example, if a business rule indicates ("customer orders of greater than $10,000 require a credit score greater than 800"), then "customer order" and "credit score" are business terms.

The work products of value streams, Business Transactions represent a measurable exchange of value either within or between organizations. A business transaction is frequently the trigger for one or more additional processes. Information about business transactions is normally managed in a data object. Examples include Invoice, Sales Order, Purchase Order, Shipping Manifest, Credit Memo, etc.

A business trend is a gradual change in the practices, expectations, or behavior of customers, competitors, suppliers, and/or partners of an enterprise. In general, a trend is a pattern of gradual change in a condition, output, or process, or an average or general tendency of a series of data points to move in a certain direction over time, represented by a line or curve on a graph. (BusinessDictionary.com)

A business unit is typically a high level division of a company. An organizational unit is a coherent set of teams and departments, usually structured in a hierarchy. While business units are composed of organization units, the terms are modeled as one element due to the nature of recursive composition.
Typically, a business is divided into organization units, each with their own set of responsibilities. The role of an organization unit is to provide resources (money, staff, infrastructure, governance) to enable business processes to occur.

Porter's Five Forces analysis looks at individual businesses or "strategic business units", examining the threats that lead to a rich understanding of the competitive and cooperative environment in which a business operates. The factors that affect buyer power are:
  • Bargaining leverage
  • Buyer volume
  • Buyer information
  • Brand identity
  • Price sensitivity
  • Threat of backward integration
  • Product differentiation
  • Buyer concentration vs. industry
  • Substitutes available
  • Buyers' incentives

A capability roadmap is a plan describing a feasible series of carefully scoped initiatives along with the sequence and estimated timelines in which those initiatives should take place, in order to achieve a business objective. Usually delivered as a document or architectural model describing the business capabilities as they are, and the changes planned over the course of a future period of time (usually one to three years).

A point in a customer process or in time where the customer interacts with the process of discovering, experiencing, acquiring, servicing, or disposing of the product.
This is specifically a touchpoint against the channel, and not the product itself. (for example, a channel touchpoint for a television set can include the retail store where they purchase it, but won't include the ease of using the remote control.)

This entity represents sales, distribution and communication channels in the business model.
Distribution channels are the mechanisms by which the customer's product or service reaches the customer. For products, the distribution channels element will describe the flow of goods from manufacturing to market, including inventory and retailing. For manufacturing organizations, this element also describes the sourcing of parts and construction of the product or products themselves. For services, this element describes the location, management, and provisioning of service resources to the customers on an as-needed basis.
Sales channels are the mechanisms by which the product or service is sold to the customer. This typically includes owned retail, owned online, partner retail, partner online, and mobile salesforce.
Communication channels include the mechanisms by which the product's availability and features are described to the customer. This includes advertising (TV, Radio, Print, Internet, Mobile, Billboard, Direct mail, In-store, In-partner-store) as well as word of mouth, event promotions, and seminars.

A charter is a legal document that defines controlling elements of the business model including relationships, products, services, customer types, and locations. The charter language for government agencies appears in one or more specific pieces of legislation.
A legal entity chartered to perform business activities. The hierarchy of business units roll up to a company. This is distinct from an enterprise that may involve the activities of many companies.
A competitive opportunity is an exploitable set of circumstances with uncertain outcome, requiring commitment of resources and involving exposure to risk. (Source: BusinessDictionary.com).

A competitive pressure is a challenge to the percieved or actual market position of a company that occurs through the offerings of competitors, the activities of regulators, or the behavior of customers, partners or suppliers.

A competitor model set is a specific set of business models typical within a particular industry. This set is used to allow comparisons using the five forces model proposed by Porter.
The construct is created solely for the purpose of comparing an enterprise to competitors (within the confines of an industry). Both the enterprise itself and its competitors may have additional business models outside the competitor model set.
In order to make a valid comparison within an industry, a set of business models typical to the industry is constructed, and the various competitors are evaluated from the standpoint of that constrained set.

The cost and revenue models represent both the costs and revenues that are indicated by the business model. This provides an understanding of what costs that the model requires and the revenues that it will generate from various channels.

A specific person or organization that has purchased the products and/or servces of the enterprise. In some organizations, the definition of "customer" is more expansive to include people and organizations that are desired or targeted prospects.

A likely series of events that describes how a customer's life and normal activities interact with a product or service, from the viewpoint of the customer. A scenario typically strings together a series of customer and channel touchpoints, in a reasonable situation, as the customer goes through an interaction to learn about, try, acquire, use, service, or dispose of a product or service.

The customer needs element describes in precise terms, the motivations that lead specific types of customers to buy or use products and services from the enterprise, and how the enterprise nurtures those motivations through marketing and support activities. Note that this is not a list of customer types, but rather a list of "customer value statements" that one or more types of customers may align to. A useful mechanism for capturing customer needs may be to consider needs from the following list:
  • Desire for outcomes
  • Values
  • Attitudes
  • Behaviors
  • Culture
  • Constraints
  • Experiences
  • Motivations

A customer type is a segment or grouping of customers based on common attributes, useful for the sake of documenting and describing shared demands, interactions, concerns, or assets. Examples: "Large volume distributor," "Merchant Bank," "Small office / home office," "General E-mail user"

A data object refers to any "thing" that a business process manipulates where a representation is stored in data. Specifically a data object is a specific composition of data elements either produced by or consumed by a business process. The data object may originate outside the organization or may be generated during the course of operations. A "business document" is a special case data object that represents 100% of the relevant information of a business transaction.

The smallest independent unit of information. Data elements may be described by attributes and properties and are typically manipulated by applications. In order for automated checks to occur validating a business rule, the systems of an enterprise must capture business terms as data elements.

Porter's Five Forces analysis looks at individual businesses or "strategic business units", examining the threats that lead to a rich understanding of the competitive and cooperative environment in which a business operates. The degree of rivalry is most likely to be high where entry is likely; there is the threat of substitute products, and suppliers and buyers in the market attempt to control. The factors that can be used to measure the degree of rivalry are
  • Exit barriers
  • Industry concentration
  • Fixed costs/Value added
  • Industry growth
  • Intermittent overcapacity
  • Product differences
  • Switching costs
  • Brand identity
  • Diversity of rivals
  • Corporate stakes

A directive is a type of standing policy or business rule that is adopted on the authority of a person or office within an enterprise. In the case of governmental institutions, a directive may originate in legislation, but it is implemented through the authority of the head of the institution (such as a minister of public lands or a secretary of the interior.).

A "driving stakeholder" is a person within an organization that owns accountability for a business strategy or objective. This person is a stakeholder to a business strategy but may also be the source of that strategy and is clearly a driving force in insuring that it comes about. To be an effective driver, a stakeholder must not only be accountable for an objective, but must have some kind of formal relationship with the person or team that is responsible for delivering on that objective.

The geographies and locales element describes the specific physical locations and contexts in which the products and services will be offered. This is a critical and necessary part of the business model as it is both enabled by, and directly impacted by, the abilities of various business partners as well as the demands of the customers. Many evaluations of a business model will focus on opportunities to extend the business through the consideration of additional geographies.

A goal group is a high level taxonomy for business goals. Sometimes called pillars, themes, or focus areas, a group of goals is usually formed as a shorthand to communicate the goals of an organization to the employees, partners, and stakeholders in a simple fashion. For example, in an annual report, a corporation may announce that, for the next year, they are focused on financial goals and on restructuring the company after a recent acquisition: two goal groups.

A governance body is an empowered group of individuals, within an enterprise, with the right to make decisions about the policies, efforts, and/or business rules of an enterprise function, capability, or process. Governance bodies are typically chartered in a formal manner with specific responsibilities, which may include
  • oversight of investment to produce specific results
  • oversight of operations to maintain controls on cost, speed, and/or quality
  • oversight of planning functions to manage change functions
  • oversight of market positioning / mergers / competitive awareness
While some governance bodies may be chartered to operate continuously, other bodies may be formed at the beginning of a project or initiative and be disbanded after that effort is completed.

A technical system where an application can be deployed. A Host may be a physical or virtual unit of hardware, or may be an instance of a virtual machine located in a "cloud" configuration (public or private).

An Industry is a classification of businesses that share the same basic value proposition and similar business models. In the context of the EBMM, Industry is the independent object to which each of the five forces applies: Degree of Rivalry, Threat of Substitutes, Barriers to Entry, Supplier Power, and Buyer Power. By recognizing that competitors may have entirely different collections of business models, an enterprise can find a method to take advantage of a competitors' liabilities.

An Influencer is anything external to the business that has the potential for affecting the ability of the organization to fulfill its business model. An influencer exists independently of the organization. It's influence may be directed at the organization (as in the case of a court of law adjudicating a lawsuit in which the organization is a plaintiff) or indirect (as in the case of a business trend that affects how customers view the products of the organization). Indirect influencers do not normally refer to the organization by name.

documentation.value: The name of the organization that the influencer is speaking on behalf of, if any.

properties.documentation: One of the elements of a business model assessment, an issue is a business judgement that captures a problem (or percieved problem) that the business would like to see addressed. The business model assessment is composed of one or more business judgements, and puts perspective around the model or models evaluated.

A high-level metric which reflects a process or characteristic that is typically measured on a business leader's scorecard. (Source Microsoft IT Quality and Business Engineering)
ITIL defines a KPI as: A Metric that is used to help manage a Process, IT Service or Activity. Many Metrics may be measured, but only the most important of these are defined as KPIs and used to actively manage and report on the Process, IT Service or Activity. KPIs should be selected to ensure that Efficiency, Effectiveness, and Cost Effectiveness are all managed

A Legislative Edict is a requirement, placed by a legislative body, forcing <u>change </u>on an organization. Typically used to regulate government agencies, legislative edicts can be placed on commercial organizations as well (example: Sarbanes-Oxley Financial Regulations). A legislative edict is different from a regulation, in that a regulation forces ongoing measurement, while an edict forces change.

A Measurement category is a taxonomy applied to process metrics (and therefore, KPIs, which are a type of process metric). By grouping metrics into categories, methods can be employed to find objectives or initiatives where the success metrics are in opposition to one another (e.g. where the outcome of one objective is to increase a particular measure while the outcome of another is to decrease the same measure).

A written declaration of an organization's core purpose and focus that normally remains unchanged over time. Properly crafted mission statements (1) serve as filters to separate what is important from what is not, (2) clearly state the common threads that bind the business models, and (3) communicate a sense of intended direction to the entire organization.
Derived. Sources: BusinessDictionary.com
Alternative definition from the OMG Business Motivation Model
A Mission indicates the ongoing operational activity of the enterprise. The Mission describes what the business is or will be doing on a day-to-day basis.
Objectives are measurable milestones that support a strategy and measure the achievement of a business goal. Objectives must be measurable and must have a target date.

documentation.value: Alias for "Strategy Perspective," the viewpoint is the identity of the abstract stakeholder concerns used to create a strategy map. Predefined perspectivies, from Kaplan and Norton, are: Financial Perspective, Customer Perspective, Internal Perspective, and Learning / Growth Perspective.

properties.documentation: A composition of products and/or services (and the prices and conditions under which they are offered), that can be individually purchased by a customer. Offerings may be available only to qualified customers as a way of packaging value for specific types of customers without undercutting other customers. Offerings may also be limited for reasons of distribution, legal concerns, localization, or available organizational or partner competencies.

An Outcomes is the Effect of an Action that is important in a Strategy, Initiative, or Scorecard. (OMG BAWG).
In the context of the the EBMM, an inititiative creates a discrete set of proposed changes, each of which maps to one or more outcome. Outcomes are measured, and usually appear as part of a business case.
When modeling a Benefits Dependency Network, we use the term Benefit for this element.

The business partner type describes the relationship between the enterprise and external entities that that cooperate to provide value.
Partner types include: suppliers, vendors, sales partners, agents, service providers, distributors, retailers, and value-added resellers.
These connections can define success for a business by allowing for specific efficiencies of capital, resources, and shared risk. They can also provide a disincentive to competition against a key parther, therefore constraining the activities and strategies of an enterprise.
A person or group of people acting as a team. This entity is included specifically to support methods that involve resource planning.

Derived from the notion of a "Balanced Scorecard," as pioneered by Kaplan and Norton, a perspective is a categorization of a business strategy or objective to one of a fixed list of "levels" of strategy, where strategies at any level support the strategies 'above" it and supported by the strategies "below" it.
The notion of a perspective is to guide the thinking of the strategist to ensure that strategies at each of the levels are considered and linked. Authors Kaplan and Norton suggest that there are four perspectives: Financial, Customer, Internal, and Learning.

A platform is a stable set of abstractions in technology on which a wide array of different types of software can be constructed. Normally composed of one or more commercial or open-source products, a platform may be expressed as a composition of both hardware and software, or may be software only (wherein it is often called a "stack"). Platforms may be built on other platforms (just as packaged ERP systems are able to run on multiple different operating systems).
Because of the recursive nature of this concept, a single element of a platform may be referred to as a technology, although the term "technology" has many other meanings that do not fit in this place in the EBMM model.

One of the elements of a business model assessment, a potential reward is a type of potential impact to the organization that should be considered as part of a business judgement. The business model assessment is composed of one or more business judgements, and puts perspective around the model or models evaluated.

A principle is any statement that is thought, by senior leadership, to be useful guidance for the organization to consider when making business decisions.
A Principle is different from a directive or policy in that a principle, by itself, has no teeth. In order for an executive to place "force of law" around a principle, they must create directives, rules, and (often) business processes that ensure that a principle is routinely followed.
The types of principles detailed in the EBMM include mission statements and vision statements, but other types of principles exist and are commonly used, including codes of conduct, preferred management approaches and design principles used in Enterprise Architecture.

A measurement collected during the operation of a business process. Setting a baseline measurement and then tracking the metric over time, with stimulation by both anticipated and surprise events, provides a mechanism for alerting the operational management teams of problems that may arise or have arisen and which may affect a key performance indicator. Normally, a KPI is a type of process metric selected for it's relationship to the value chain.

A concept in customer scenario modeling, a product touchpoint is a generalized element in a model of the customer interation with a product. At a touchpoint, the experience of a customer can impact the setup, use, storage, and disposal of a product and/or service.
In the EBMM, a product touchpoint is specifically a touchpoint against the product itself, and not the channel through which it is purchased. (for example, a product touchpoint for a television set can include the packaging, the remote control, and the tilt pedestal, but won't include the retail store where a customer purchased the television set.)

This element of the business model contains a description of the specific products and/or services offered by the business. It is important to recognize that the specific products or services developed must derive from customer demands in order to effectively provide value. This relationship, between customers demands and the products offered, is the central focus of marketing in many organizations.

A project can be defined as a temporary endeavor undertaken to create a unique product or service.
Projects are different from other ongoing operations in an organization because unlike operations, projects have a definite beginning and an end - they have a limited duration. Projects are critical to the realization of performing organization's business strategy because projects are a means by which the initiatives of the company are implemented.
Projects typically involve doing or creating unique outcomes, and are therefore each one is unique. A product or service may be unique even if the category to which it belongs is large. For example, although several residential complexes have been built in the past, creation of a new house will be a project because each individual facility is unique - different location, design, resources working, owners etc. (Source PMI)

A specific proposed change to the business that occurs through the mechanism of a business initiative. The business change should be framed in terms of the effect that it will have on the maturity of a business unit capability. A proposed change is a type of "action" for which the intended "effect" is a measurable outcome.

One of the elements of a business model assessment, a recommendation of change is a business judgement that indicates suggested changes to a business model or level of business maturity needed to address the effects of an influencer. The business model assessment is composed of one or more business judgements, and puts perspective around the model or models evaluated.

A regulation is a requirement placed on the organization by a legislative or regulatory body. This is not an influencer in the sense that an organization does not have the right to ignore the regulation. That said, the organization is not "governed" by the regulation directly, but by business policies aligned to comply with the regulation.

An area or group of business capabilities where the business must excel in order for this business model to be successful. This is a general concept, not a specific grouping of business capabilities. This part of the business model drives the need for specific business unit capabilities to perform at higher-than-average levels of effectiveness and efficiency.

Part of a business model, a resource can represent anything that the business must employ, possess, or control in order to deliver on a required competency. Examples of a resource may be:
  • a person or group of people able to fulfill a particular role or mission
  • a building, office, suite, or store in which some activities are performed
  • a physical asset used in the process of fulfilling a capability
  • materials or inputs to manufacturing
  • inventory of goods to be sold or distributed
  • inventory of services ready to be provisioned or provided
  • cash or equities
  • Intellectual Property

One of the elements of a business model assessment, a risk is a type of potential impact to the organization that should be considered as part of a business judgement. The business model assessment is composed of one or more business judgements, and puts perspective around the model or models evaluated.

A service level agreement is a contract made between two business units, where one business unit provides a service to another. The contract describes specific measures by which the service provider's performance will be measured, as well as acceptable ranges of those measures that the consumer would find acceptable.
A discrete part of a software application. A component may be deployed one or more times, on one or more hosts, as part of a distributed system.

One of the elements of a business model assessment, a strength or weakness is a business judgement that reflects expert opinions about the performance of the business according to a model of performance being used by the assessor. The business model assessment is composed of one or more business judgements, and puts perspective around the model or models evaluated.

A success metric is a measurable value or range of values that a key performance indicator may fall into. It that describes, in quantifiable terms, the successful outcome of a strategy or business initiative.
One type of Success Metric is a CTQ. A CTQ (Critical to Quality) is the measureable aspect of the customer experience that is addressed by a process improvement project. The CTQs are identified as a result of gathering the Voice of the Customer.
alias: Critical To Quality (CTQ), Customer Input KPI, Success Metric, Target Measure

An analysis based on Porter's Five Forces looks at individual businesses or "strategic business units", examining the threats that lead to a rich understanding of the competitive and cooperative environment in which a business operates. The power of suppliers tends to be a reversal of the power of buyers.
  • Where the switching costs are high e.g. Switching from one software supplier to another.
  • Power is high where the brand is powerful e.g. Cadillac, Pizza Hut, Microsoft.
  • There is a possibility of the supplier integrating forward e.g. Brewers buying bars.
  • Customers are fragmented (not in clusters) so that they have little bargaining power e.g. Gas/Petrol stations in remote places.
The factors that affect supplier power are:
  • Supplier concentration
  • Importance of volume to supplier
  • Differentiation of inputs
  • Impact of inputs on cost or differentiation
  • Switching costs of firms in the industry
  • Presence of substitute inputs
  • Threat of forward integration
  • Cost relative to total purchases in industry

A system interaction point is a specific point in a business process where contact occurs between people and systems. In some methods, a survey of use cases would start with the list of system interaction points that apply to a particular system.
Note that a system interaction can involve more than one system at the same interaction point. An example would be where a customer is entered into a customer management system, producing the customer id, and then an order is entered into another system referencing the customer id.
The presence of a system interaction point drives the need for an application feature. Where a proposed change is driven by a business initiative, that change could potentially drive changes to zero, one, or more system interaction points. Those changes would impact applications.

A required measurable attribute of software that describes a desired level of quality for a system. These are requirements to meet performance levels of Availability, Efficiency, Flexibility, Integrity, Interoperability, Maintainability, Portability, Reliability. Reusability, Robustness, Testability, and Usability. These attributes are known as System Quality Attributes by the SEI ATAM method.
Selecting the relative priority of measurable attributes for a single system often requires tradeoffs. These priorities are best set by the system's customer.

Porter's Five Forces analysis looks at individual businesses or "strategic business units", examining the threats that lead to a rich understanding of the competitive and cooperative environment in which a business operates.
  • Where there is product-for-product substitution e.g. email for fax Where there is substitution of need e.g. better toothpaste reduces the need for dentists.
  • Where there is generic substitution (competing for the currency in your pocket) e.g. Video suppliers compete with travel companies.
  • We could always do without e.g. cigarettes.

A tool feature is an abstract representation of the ability of a tool to meet the specific needs of a business process at a system interaction point. Features are describable, testable, and perceivable by the users of the tool. Application features tend to be information-oriented while physical tools (like machines, vehicles, or even furniture) tends to be oriented to the physical measurement, management, manipulation, or manufacturing of an item.

A use case is an artifact of system analysis that defines a sequence of actions and events that a solution is expected to perform, yielding an observable result of value to a particular actor.
The use case contains main, alternative, and exception flows of events. The functionality of a system is defined by different use cases, each of which represents a specific flow of events. The description of a use case defines what happens in the system when the use case is performed.
Although a user story inhabits the same positiion in the EBMM, a user story is a simpler flow. It is a single discrete set of actions and events produced during an agile software development process.
Typically, a software development project will chose to use either use cases or user stories, not both.

documentation.value: the back-and-forth steps taken by an individual actor when engaging with a software system to consume one feature of that system. A use case scenario is part of a use case, which is a mechanism for describing software requirements. It is not a business process, nor a thread through a business process, and should not be confused with one. The preferred mapping is: one or more use cases are used to capture the requirements for a single process activity.

properties.documentation:
A value chain is a term used to refer to a model of value streams related to a single enterprise. Defined by Michael Porter, a value chain breaks out the various value streams into categories.
Note that a value chain typically divides value streams into two types: core and supporting. A single value stream may map to more than one category of core or more than one category of supporting, but rarely into both core and supporting.
While Porter defined a generic model, industry specific models exist that reflect terminology and processes of different industries.

The central notion of a business model, the value proposition describes how the enterprise, through its activities, adds value to the consumer or marketplace. The Value proposition binds together the notions of customer demands, required competencies, revenue models and business partnerships. It is a statement from the viewpoint of the target customers that informs everyone "why" the business' products and services are valuable.

A value stream is a sequence of business processes the boundaries of which are typically defined by business transactions. They represent end-to-end sequences such as "order to cash" or "idea to available product."

A value system is a model illustrating the interactions of value streams in one or more suppliers, the value chain(s) of the enterprise itself, and the downstream channel partners all the way to the consumer of the enterprise' goods.
A value system illustrates the relative position of the enterprise in a larger system that provides value. In many cases, the end customer may not be aware of the incremental value provided by any one enterprise. An example may be an air freight company, in their value system with retailers. End customers may not be aware that the freight company was ever involved.

A vision is a statement or compound group of statements that describes the desired state of success for an enterprise. It is often described from the viewpoint of the customers or stakeholders. For example, a retailer of electronics could describe their vision as follows: "to be the most trusted, reliable, and cost-competitive source of electronic products in the Greater Seattle area."
Alternative definition from the OMG Business Motivation Model: A Vision describes the future state of the enterprise, without regard to how it is to be achieved. A Vision is the ultimate, possibly unattainable, state the enterprise would like to achieve. A Vision is often compound, rather than focused toward one particular aspect of the business problem.

A collection of business terms that are commonly used by the communities of business practitioners within an enterprise. Many organizations have an informal vocabulary, while a few have made the effort to define terms in a common manner.

This section will contain a list of "key questions" that senior leaders in an organization seek to have answered. For each key question, a view of the EBMM will be extracted reflecting the elements that can be used to answer that question. As an organization seeks to implement a metamodel, they should consider which of these key questions they would seek to answer, and include those views in their instantiation of the EBMM.
Classification of People or organizations who benefit from the service

Regulated Resources: (1) People or companies whose actions are restrained or prevented by the actions of a government service (criminals are regulated by the services of the police) (2) natural resources or geographic areas governed and managed by the government.

Consider:
For a regulatory service, is the regulator channel the same as the delivery channel? Is there a need for two objects here?

documentation.value: a brand perception is said to "overlay" an offering in that the customers perception of the brand will impact how they perceive an offering and the value that they expect to get from it. The two elements are distinct, however, in that an offering is very transitive and represents something that a customer can buy, while a brand perception may be built up over time.

A brand perception could be said to overlay an instance of a business model, as offered by a particular enterprise, in that the perception influences how the customer expects to collect value from the products and services offered by a particular business model of an enterprise.
BAWG discussion 5-13-11, objectives are statements of being that collectively meet the goal. The verb 'quantifies' is inherited from the OMG BMM.

Business judgements are compiled into a business model assessment for the purpose of indicating how the business model can or should change in order to meet the changing needs of the marketplace, customers, and competitive forces.

Note that one customer can behave as many different customer types. However, in each of the needs met by the enterprise, they are behaving in a single customer type in order for the enterprise to meet their needs. Therefore, a single customer may have many relationships with an enterprise and may purchase diverse products or services while behaving as more than one customer type.
