properties.name: Primary View
properties.documentation:
The Primary view illustrates each of the elements that are considered centrral to the EBMM. It does not show auxiliary elements which are useful for understanding how the EBMM relates to other areas of the business, and it does not include elements that are "taxonomies only" for the sake of clarity. This decision is purely visual and is not reflective of the relative importance of excluded elements.
The background areas reflect subsets of elements that "roll up" when looking at the EBMM at a higher level. The components illustrated with a thick black outline are the core elements in each of these subsets. Most of the other elements with an area are directly related to that core element.
In the case of business model, the business model is composed of most of the other elements within that area. In the case of Directive, the other elements are specific instances of directives.

properties.name: IT Traceability Viewpoint
properties.documentation:
One set of stakeholders for the EBMM is the IT program itself. For those IT planning stakeholders that wish to reflect the connection between business models, capabilities, drivers, processes and requirements, this view is helpful. The entire "design" view is a subset of this viewpoint.
The key difference between this viewpoint and the planning viewpoint is that it is used to illustrate the traceability of IT efforts with the pivot being the IT effort itself (Applications and Requirements). In effect, the need to demonstrate traceability is often an exercise in justification. Reports and models aligned with this viewpoint are sufficient to demonstrate that justification.

properties.name: Requirements Viewpoint
properties.documentation: One set of stakeholders for the EBMM is the IT program itself. For those IT programs that wish to reflect the connection between business drivers, processes and requirements, this view is helpful. Note that this viewpoint is overly simplistic. That is intentional to make life easier for IT architects and engineers. It is the experience of this model's author that the value of connecting any of the IT elements to business architecture elements other than the listed ones produces diminishing returns at best.

properties.name: Planning Viewpoint
properties.documentation: The planning viewpoint illustrates the elements relevant to the needs of business units (and usually their IT groups) accountable for taking the drivers and producing a roadmap that illustrates how the business will change to meet those needs. Normally, the needs of alignment can be met using views from this viewpoint.

properties.name: Service Management Viewpoint
properties.documentation: The service management view brings into context the additional elements of a service level agreement, and the taxonomies of business processes and capabilities. This is useful for stakeholders involved in planning and management of business services. Note that the actual business service managers need additional elements that are outside the scope of the EBMM.

properties.name: Business Model Viewpoint
properties.documentation:
The business model view illustrates the key elements needed to understand the business model. Note that you do not need to actually have a customer in order to have a business model, but it is often useful, when describing a model, to refer to actual customers to "make it real" to the business stakeholders.
This set of attributes directly relates to the work of Alexander Osterwalder but the relationships are somewhat different in that the EBMM breaks down the attributes based on the needs of an enterprise architecture team to collect the information across an enterprise. Osterwalder's work is primarily useful for creating business model assessments, so the needs he describes are less rigorous.
Note that the Business Model Canvas from Osterwalder's book is a good example of a tool that is useful for discussing (and innovating) on the idea of a business model. The data collected through that tool could be captured in a data structure built on this metamodel without modification. In that way, we can say that the Business Model Canvas is a VIEW on this metamodel.
The key to understanding the business model viewpoint is to recognize that most of these elements are part of the business model itself. The business model is a unique composition of these elements designed to produce a unique value proposition. The stakeholders of a business model view would be strategic advisors and company executives seeking to generate new business strategies.
For commercial organizations, fully realized business model views are not normally exposed in public except in filings with regulatory bodies (like the Securities and Exchange Commission in the US). For governmental organizations, these elements are usually described in the legislation and regulations that describe the responsibilities of the organization.

properties.name: Strategy Viewpoint
properties.documentation:
Strategies are the real motivators of business behavior. This model is an indirect derivative of the OMG Business Motivation Model. This illustration puts strategy into the context of other elements within the model.
A view produced in accordance with this viewpoint would illustrate the relationships between the various elements of motivation, normally to demonstrate alignment between a proposed change and all of the drivers and influencers that demand that change to occur.
Note that drivers do not have a direct relationship to directives. That is because the decision to implement a driver is independent of the driver itself. In other words, a policy ignored is still a policy. The decision to implement it would require a business objective, and from that, a success metric to be defined.

properties.name: Business Capability Viewpoint
properties.documentation: This viewpoint brings in the concepts of Business Program, Asset, and Company into the context of the EBMM core elements. The notion of a business program is of direct interest to stakeholders of an Enterprise Program Management Office (EPMO).

properties.name: Business Process Viewpoint
properties.documentation: This simple viewpoint illustrates the relationships between business units, processes, metrics and strategies, including the relationship with rules and capabilities. This is a direct adoption of the connection for business rules from the OMG BMM, which was in turn derived from the work of the business rules group. Note that this model is not sufficient for full business process modeling. A business process model viewpoint is outside the scope of business architecture, and therefore is not included in the EBMM.

properties.name: Business Model Assessment Viewpoint
properties.documentation:
This viewpoint illustrates the relationship of a business model assessment to the rest of the elements of the business motivation model. Business model assessments can be performed either by internal parties or external parties. By documenting the assessment in the model, we illustrate two things. A) an assessment is not, by itself, a driver. Assessments do not force change. However, an assessment can be the justification for change.
This assessment is fundamentally different from the assessment of capability maturity. A business model assessment is designed to show the business how their models work in the marketplace. They are external in focus and may question the structure of an existing business model. A capability assessment is designed to show how well the organization is aligned to fulfill the model. A capability assessment does not question that the business should have a particular model, but rather how well the company can perform it.

properties.name: Core Elements Only View
properties.documentation: The core elements only view is used as a foundation for creating "management graphics" that allow the EBMM to be explained to non-architects. It is not directly presented to management. It can be useful when introducing an architect to the EBMM.

properties.name: Enterprise Strategy Viewpoint
properties.documentation:
This viewpoint is useful to focus on the relationship between strategies, processes, and metrics. Any strategy that is not described in terms of a success metric is not actionable. Therefore, it is the job of the business architect to insure that strategies either break down to objectives that can be measured or directly contain the metrics.
Not all success metrics can be directly tracked by the business. Some need an internal metric that serves as a proxy for the actual success metric. That is a Key Performance Indicator. In those cases where a business objective can be directly described by an internal success metric, then the KPI is the same as the success metric (the metric tracks itself).
Note that a KPI is a process metric, but not all process metrics are KPIs. You can measure many things about a process. There can be many reasons for measurement. However, some metrics are purely supporting, and would not be a metric useful for tracking success.

properties.name: Structural View
properties.documentation: The structural view illustrates only the static relationships between elements of different types. It is primarily useful for folks considering using Domain Driven Design to create or configure tools to perform EA activities.

properties.name: Package Oriented Implementation Viewpoint
properties.documentation: This viewpoint exists to illustrate how ERP implementations can benefit from the EBMM metamodel. In an ERP implementation, a capability analysis can indicated the changes to business processes, but after that, business process is the key. You work to match the needs of the process to the "capabilties" of the ERP system. (The EBMM term is "Application Feature" but for this view, we are using an alias of "Application Capability" to improve understanding for this stakeholder community).

properties.name: Microsoft IT subset
properties.documentation: Microsoft IT does not use the Enterprise Business Motivation Model. However, the metamodel that is used within Microsoft IT is a well-aligned subset of the EBMM illustrated in this model.

properties.name: EITA Viewpoint
properties.documentation: Enterprise IT Architecture is a subset of Enterprise Architecture, specifically focused on the complexity involved with information technology. Many Enterprise Architects focus on this area exclusively, leaving the rest of the areas to business architects.

properties.name: Customer Viewpoint
properties.documentation:
Customers are the life blood of any commercial enterprise, and this section is rather specifically tailored to commercial organizations. That said, governmental and non-profit organizations may view their stakeholders as customers, but the relationships are unlikely to be the same. Further work is taking place on the EBMM to create a view that is better tailored to the kinds of relationships typical in government settings.
Terms specific to the customer viewpoint are not terms used by the customer, but rather terms used by the enterprise to understand, communicate with, and develop solutions to the needs of the customer. The growth of Enterprise Architecture into a richer understanding of customers, their needs and enterprise responses to changes in those needs has been a major focus of EA activity in the years between 2008 and 2014.

properties.name: What capabilities are impacted by strategic direction
What programs are more strategically important than others
How do we discover, catalog, and quantify architectural risks, and assign them to business leaders to be addressed?
How will the organization look when it is architecturally mature?
What options exist for the design of the organization?
How do you measure or predict the business value of shared services or standardized processes?
For each process area, how should the process owner decide what level of integration and standardization to target?
What business units are operating outside of process owners' express intent for standardization and integration?
What factors drive the cost of a business process?
How do we visualize the agility and flexibility of a business?
How do we align the measures of the business to the measures of IT?
How do we align IT efforts to business priorities?
properties.documentation:
Business Strategies are a type of business driver. They can appear in hierarchies or in a list with dependencies. Business initiatives should be mapped to the driver that motivates its existence. (any business initiative not mapped to a driver is not aligned, and the priority of the business initiative should derive from a balance of architectural risk, value of the strategy, and value of the proposed changes).
Business initiatives suggest changes to business processes. All IT impacts can be found by looking for the system interaction points (process steps that interact with system features).

properties.name: Do we have or plan to have the process, system, and information maturity that the business needs to meet their strategic needs?
What current or upcoming technologies do we need to invest in?
Which platforms have overlapping or redundant features?
Are there dependencies between applications and information that can create obstacles to successful project delivery?
What business capabilities must be improved in order to improve our competitiveness?
Are significant areas of system or process weakness garnering the necessary investment needed to reduce risk of failure, disruption, or breach?
properties.documentation: Starting with the list of architectural risks identified through maturity assessments, a report can be generated to highlight the capabilities with total architectural risks above a specific threshold. A gap report can be produced if there are no programs or proposed changes targeting those capabilites or if the total investment provided is less than 60% of the total investment required.
